claims.statement: Supervised ASR models fine-tuned on a single dataset distribution achieve low WER on that distribution but fail to generalize, making many more errors than humans on other distributions.
claims.scope: Quantified for LibriSpeech-trained models evaluated on 12 other academic datasets

claims.statement: Large-scale weakly supervised pretraining on 680,000 hours of diverse internet audio enables zero-shot transfer to diverse speech recognition benchmarks without any dataset-specific fine-tuning.
claims.scope: Evaluated on 13 academic ASR datasets including diverse domains and acoustic conditions

claims.statement: Despite matching a top supervised LibriSpeech model on its home benchmark (both at 2.7% WER), zero-shot Whisper Large V2 achieves 55.2% average relative error reduction over that supervised model on 13 other datasets.
claims.scope: Comparison with wav2vec 2.0 Large (no LM) on 13 OOD datasets; text normalization applied

claims.statement: Zero-shot Whisper's robustness matches human robustness: the robustness frontier of zero-shot Whisper includes the 95% confidence interval of human performance on the studied datasets.
claims.scope: Single human evaluator (Alec) in Figure 2; 25 audio recordings in Kincaid46 for Figure 7

claims.statement: A single multitask token-based format enables one model to perform multilingual transcription, speech-to-English translation, voice activity detection, language identification, and time-aligned transcription without architectural changes.
claims.scope: All five tasks demonstrated; performance varies by task

claims.statement: Whisper performance scales reliably with model size for multilingual speech recognition, translation, and language identification, but English speech recognition shows diminishing returns consistent with approaching human-level saturation.
claims.scope: Five model sizes 39M-1550M parameters; saturation interpretation is the authors' inference

claims.statement: Zero-shot Whisper performance scales with training dataset size across all tasks, with approximately power-law improvement in WER for multilingual SR and log-linear improvement in translation BLEU.
claims.scope: Tested at 0.5%-100% of 680k-hour dataset on medium-sized model; full dataset shows some diminishing returns

claims.statement: For small models, joint multilingual and multitask training degrades English speech recognition compared to English-only training; for large models, joint training eventually yields positive transfer with slightly better English SR performance.
claims.scope: Compute-adjusted comparison; 95% bootstrap CI shown in Figure 9

claims.statement: Whisper achieves near-human English ASR performance: on 25 Kincaid46 recordings, pure-human transcription services are only a fraction of a percentage point better, and a computer-assisted service is 1.15 WER points better.
claims.scope: 25 recordings from Kincaid46; 5 services compared; no confidence intervals reported

claims.statement: Whisper zero-shot achieves a new SOTA of 29.1 BLEU on CoVoST2 X->en translation, improving over mSLAM by 6.7 BLEU on the lowest-resource language group.
claims.scope: Zero-shot evaluation; text standardizer applied. Authors caution against SOTA claim due to normalizer.

claims.statement: Zero-shot Whisper outperforms all compared open-source ASR models and most commercial ASR services on long-form transcription across 7 datasets.
claims.scope: 7 long-form datasets; 4 commercial services as of September 2022; commercial services may have been trained on some of these datasets

claims.statement: The amount of per-language training data strongly predicts zero-shot speech recognition performance (r^2=0.83 on log-log scale), with WER halving for every 16-fold increase in training hours.
claims.scope: Evaluated across languages in Fleurs dataset; outliers include languages with unique scripts

claims.statement: Language identification performance is not competitive with supervised methods (64.5% vs 77.7% on Fleurs), but this comparison is confounded because Whisper has no training data for 20 of 102 Fleurs languages; on the 82 overlapping languages, Whisper achieves 80.3%.
claims.scope: Fleurs dataset; supervised models trained specifically on these languages

limitations.statement: The supervised models in this comparison are all trained primarily on LibriSpeech; other supervised baselines may generalize differently.
Zero-shot transfer may be enabled by data contamination rather than generalization; de-duplication was applied for TED-LIUM 3 only.
Fine-tuning performance not studied; Whisper may benefit further from domain-specific fine-tuning.
Text normalization co-developed with Whisper; comparison on some datasets (WSJ, CallHome, Switchboard) may favor Whisper.
Human comparison uses limited samples (25 recordings, single human in Figure 2) without confidence intervals; human panel not a representative sample.
Language identification significantly underperforms supervised SOTA; translation performance weaker on high-resource languages.
Scaling analysis uses medium-sized models for data scaling; LLM-style scaling laws not fully characterized.
Text standardizer used for translation; prevents direct comparison or SOTA claims per authors' own caution.
Commercial ASR services may have been trained on some of the long-form evaluation datasets; comparison not necessarily fair.
Outlier languages (non-Indo-European, unique scripts) deviate from the scaling trend for reasons not fully diagnosed.
